name: Strontium supplements
short: Case report: DRESS drug reaction with strontium citrate. High-dose citrate by mouth: fetal bone, eye anomalies in rats. Prescription ranelate (postmenopausal women): data suggest slightly more clots.
text: The cited sources on non-prescription strontium supplements are case reports, a small observational study and laboratory or animal studies, and a 2016 case report notes that no controlled trials have been conducted on the effectiveness of these supplements for osteoporosis. A published case report describes drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome with granulomatous dermatitis associated with strontium citrate; no abstract is available, so only its title is cited. In pregnant rats, strontium citrate given by mouth at the highest dose tested caused anomalies of the bones and eyes in the fetuses, which the authors interpret as an adverse effect of high-dose strontium citrate on embryonic and fetal development (animal study). A laboratory study found that some supplements contain more strontium than their labels state and that high strontium concentrations added to plasma samples falsely raised total calcium test results, while ionised calcium tests were not significantly affected. In 10 women monitored while taking strontium supplements, bone strontium levels kept rising for over 4 years and varied widely between individuals; the abstract does not report adverse events. Strontium ranelate, a prescription medicine and a different form from the supplements, was reviewed in a Cochrane analysis of randomised trials in postmenopausal women: it increased diarrhoea, and additional data suggested slightly higher risks of venous thromboembolism (2.2% versus 1.5%), pulmonary embolism (0.8% versus 0.4%), seizures, memory loss and disturbance in consciousness over 3 to 4 years, although adverse events leading to withdrawal were not significantly increased. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
